messages.subject: German POS tagger and corpora
messages.subject_clean: German POS tagger and corpora
messages.body_plain:
First, two questions and then the motivation for the questions:

(1) Is TreeTagger a good POS tagger for German? Others?
(2) Is the Database of Spoken German a good corpus for spontaneously spoken German?

Motivation for first question:
I'm helping an MA student with some POS tagging in German. I've successfully used the koRpus package

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/koRpus/index.html

which uses the TreeTagger POS tagger

http://www.cis.uni-muenchen.de/~schmid/tools/TreeTagger/

to tag a sample sentence in German (that Google Translate helped me make). I'm wondering what other POS taggers for German corpus-linguistics-R-ists on this list have experience with.

Motivation for second question:
Also, another professor suggested that the student use the Database of Spoken German

http://dgd.ids-mannheim.de/

as the source for spontaneous spoken German for his study. As I don't study German (I'm merely providing the corpus linguistics support), I'm wondering if another (publicly available) corpus might be better, etc.

Thanks in advance for any words of wisdom.

messages.subject: Concordance of multi-word units
messages.subject_clean: Concordance of multi-word units
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm writing a script that will allow me to retrieve concordance for the Dutch substitutive construction "in plaats van" (i.e. "in place of"). Since this construction allows for syntactic manipulation such as interpolation, omission of the last preposition etc., I needed regular expressions to retrieve all the types of that construction. Here follows the lines of code I tried:

#### The following lines will serve to make a concordance of an unannotated text file.

corpus.files.dutch<-choose.files() # open all the corpus files of Dutch texts selected from the Project Gutenberg

all.matches.ipv<-vector() # reserve a data structure for the results

for(i in 1:length(corpus.files.dutch)) {
cat(i, "\n") # output a progress report
current.corpus.file<-scan(corpus.files.dutch[i], what="char", sep="\n", quiet=T) # to access the individual values of the vector since we need the counter
current.matches.ipv<-grep("in (de|mijn|je|jouw|uw|zijn|haar|onze|jullie|hun)? pla[ae]ts (van|der|den)?", current.corpus.file, ignore.case=T, perl=T, value=T)
if(length(current.matches.ipv)==0) { next }
all.matches.ipv<-append(all.matches.ipv, current.matches.ipv)
}

When I run the script in R, it only retrieves matches for the type "in de plaats (van)", when it should also have returned matches for many other types. The regular expression which seems problematic is higlighted.

I thank you in advance for your comments and suggestions!

C. Bechet.

messages.body_plain:
When I run the following

####################
ccf <- c("Ik heb alleen mijn plicht gedaan,' zeide ik: 'en ieder
fatsoenlijk man zou in mijn plaats evenzoo gehandeld hebben.",

         "hij heeft den Geuzenpenning afgedaan en draagt in plaats
daarvan, zeer in het oog vallend, een rozenkrans van gouden kralen en

een rijk versierd kruis.",

         "Als hij gemeend heeft dat er een abuis in de opgave des

afstands is, daar het wel drie uren zal zijn in plaats van twee,",

         "Wat hij niet tasten kon, het was de stille uitstorting des

gemoeds, die in haar plaats had;")
exact.matches("in (de|mijn|je|jouw|uw|zijn|haar|onze|jullie|hun)?

pla[ae]ts (van|der|den)?",

              ccf, case.sens=FALSE)
####################

I get matches in ccf[1] and ccf[4], namely
"in mijn plaats "
   and
"in haar plaats "

First, note that you're effectively asking for two spaces:
- at the beginning after in
- before "pla"
which you probably don't want.

Second, what you think should be matched in ccf[2] doesn't get matched
because of "daarvan", which is not in your search expression. Thus,
this works:

####################
exact.matches("in ?(de|mijn|je|jouw|uw|zijn|haar|onze|jullie|hun)?
pla[ae]ts ((daar)?van|der|den)?",
              ccf, case.sens=FALSE)
# $`Exact matches`
# [1] "in mijn plaats "   "in plaats daarvan" "in plaats van"     "in
haar plaats "
# $`Locations of matches (lines)`
# [1] 1 2 3 4
# etc.
####################

HTH,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries

Univ. of California, Santa Barbara

messages.body_plain:
While I'm not aware of an argument in TreeTagger to change the output, you can do some good old-fashioned text manipulation on the tabular data format returned by TreeTagger. Here's a toy example:

# resulting tabular data from TreeTagger
tagged <- data.frame(
  word = c("The", "TreeTagger", "is", "easy", "to", "use", "."),
  pos = c("DT", "NP", "VBZ", "JJ", "TO", "VB", "SENT"),
  lemma = c("the", "TreeTagger", "be", "easy", "to", "use", ".")
)

# good old-fashioned text manipulation
with(tagged, paste0(word, "_", pos, " ", collapse = ""))

# or with angled brackets
with(tagged, paste0(word, "<", pos, "> ", collapse = ""))

messages.subject: How to coerce a big list into a data frame
messages.subject_clean: How to coerce a big list into a data frame
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I'm trying to convert a lemmatized corpus into a data frame. In the corpus, every line shows instances of a spelling variant and its lemmas. Each line counts 8 words. It looks more like a dictionary without POS tags.

First, in order for each word in each line to appear in a separate column, I needed to split the file at every space:

> text.file<-scan(file=choose.files(), what="char", sep="\n", quiet=T)
> text.file.2<-strsplit(text.file, " ")
> head(text.file.2)
[[1]]
[1] "@"                   "@"                   "@"                   "_o:I222p30601.SBH06"
[5] "Markup(samp)"        "-"                   "-"                   "-"

[[2]]
[1] "Wj"  "wj"  "wj"  "wij" "404" "-"   "-"   "-"

[[3]]
[1] "scepenne_" "scepenne_" "scepennen" "schepen"   "014"       "-"         "-"         "-"

[[4]]
[1] "ghemeinlech" "ghemeinlech" "ghemeinlech" "gemeenlijk"  "100"         "-"           "-"
[8] "-"

Then, things get complicated. If I used the following code, it would take ages before I get everything stored into a file (text.file.2 is a large list of 399,990 elements):

for(i in 1:length(text.file.2)) {
  text.file.3<-text.file.2[[i]]
  cat(text.file.3, file=choose.files(), sep="\t", append=T)
}

Do you have an idea of how I could let R do the storing work?

Best regards and many thanks to the person/people who will be helpful in a way or another.

C. Bechet

messages.body_plain:
Just one thing: in using write.csv, the output in my spreadsheet is only one column grouping everything separated by a comma. So, instead of write.csv, I used write.table, which gave me the desired output. For every soul interested in what was aiming at, I paste the lines of code here.

# 1) Create a list with a few examples from the text file

token.lemma.pos.grouping<-list(c("@", "@", "@", "_o:I222p30601.SBH06", "Markup(samp)", "-" , "-", "-"), c("Wj",  "wj",  "wj",  "wij" ,"404", "-" ,  "-" ,  "-"  ))

# 2) Convert the list into a data frame so that each vector of the list gets its own row

token.lemma.pos.1<- data.frame(matrix(unlist(token.lemma.pos.grouping), nrow=length(token.lemma.pos.grouping), byrow=T), stringsAsFactors=FALSE)

# 3) Reduce the columns to those containing token, lemma and pos only

token.lemma.pos.2<-token.lemma.pos.1[,c(1, 4, 5)]

# 4) Save the output to a file. If necessary, rename each column header

write.table(token.lemma.pos.2, file=choose.files(), sep="\t", quote=F, col.names=c("TOKEN", "LEMMA", "POS"), row.names=F)

Assuming you don't need the list for other purposes, you could also read your data in as a data frame directly:

test.file <- read.delim(choose.file(), sep=" ")

read.delim takes a delimited table (here: whitespace), with one case per line, and interprets the first line as a header (as header=T is the default). This assumes that all lines (i.e. all your entries) have an equal number of column values, but all other solutions suggested so far would assume that, too.

Then proceed from there (like creating dataframes with certain columns, saving back to file etc.)
